text: Last lesson pinned down which environment. This lesson pins down the last piece: the specific run-time parameters — random seed, shot count, backend version — without which 'reproduce this result' is still underspecified even with the first two solved.

This lesson covers why a random seed alone isn't enough, a structured metadata record to attach to every reported experimental result, how to record seeds across multiple layers without missing one, and why real-hardware runs need a calibration timestamp instead of a seed.

A fixed simulator seed makes a specific run's shot-by-shot outcomes reproducible, given a specific version of that simulator package. If the simulator's internal pseudorandom algorithm changes between versions, the same seed on a different version can produce different sampled outcomes — which means the seed and the exact backend version have to be recorded together, neither one alone is sufficient. A full pipeline often has more than one source of randomness: a simulator seed controlling sampling, a transpiler seed controlling layout and routing heuristics that affect which circuit structure actually runs, and in a hybrid variational algorithm, the classical optimizer's own separate seed.

Attach a structured record like this to every reported result, ideally generated programmatically rather than typed by hand, so it can't silently drift from what actually ran. It captures the git commit, the experiment tag, the SDK name and version, the backend name, both the simulator and transpiler seeds, the shot count, and a timestamp. Committing this file alongside the tagged commit means every piece needed for reproduction lives in one retrievable place.

Real hardware has no seed in the simulator sense — physical noise isn't seeded pseudorandomness, it's a property of the device's current calibration state, which drifts over time. For hardware runs, record the calibration timestamp instead — when the backend's error rates were last calibrated — since that's the piece of context that actually explains why a hardware result might differ between two runs on the same backend weeks apart.

For a GHZ fidelity experiment, the complete reproducible record requires the git tag identifying the code, the lockfile identifying the environment, and this lesson's experiment record identifying the seeds and shot count. Any one of these three missing makes the result non-reproducible even if the other two are present — they're jointly necessary, not independently sufficient. Next lesson is a hands-on lab: assemble all three layers for one real experiment, then actually attempt to reproduce it as a stranger would, six months later.
